newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA GOVT SAYS CHANGES FRANKING CREDIT RULE.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA GOVT SAYS CHANGES FRANKING CREDIT RULE.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello said on Friday the government would alter its controversial 1997/98 budget proposal to severely restrict the use of dividend franking credits.
Costello said a number of changes would be made to a proposal to immediately remove franking credits from investors who hedged within 45 days of buying the stock.
As a result, the 45-day rule would only take effect from July 1, 1997, instead of the original date of May 13, 1997, when the budget was handed down, Costello said in a statement.
The changes follow recommendations made by Treasury and the Australian Tax Office.
"Arising from consultation, a number of changes will be made in relation to the 45-day rule and as a result the commencement of the measure will be deferred to 1 July 1997," Costello said.
"This later date of effect satisfies industry concerns that the new rule take effect from the beginning of the financial year."
But he said other measures to prevent trading in franking credits and dividend streaming would continue to apply from May 13.
Under the changes, fund managers that passed a "delta measurement test", where an average yield was to be be calculated, would be allowed to hedge within the 45-day period.
"Where the net equity risk is such that the net delta of the derivative is less than point-seven, the arrangement will not attract the risk diminution aspect of the 45-day rule," Costello said.
"The revised formulation provides a basis for distinguishing between legitimate commercial hedging and franking credit trading."
Institutional investors facing substantial compliance difficulties would be able to use one of three formula caps as an alternative to the 45-day rule.

"Under this alternative approach, eligible taxpayers will compare the actual franked return on a portfolio with a franked return on a benchmark portfolio consistent with the taxpayer's net equity exposure," an attachment to Costello's statement said.
"This approach bascially requires that the ratio of franking rebates to equity exposure be within a specified limit," it said.
"The taxpayer will lose any rebates in excess of the rebates allowed by the ratio."

The changes also meant individual shareholders claiming an annual franking rebate of A$2,000 or less would be exempt from the rule, as would employee share schemes for companies wholly-owned by non-resident or tax exempt shareholders.

The original plan's main objective was to remove the appeal of "dividend washing" schemes where franking credits on stocks held by foreigners are made available to local investors who use them to reduce their overall tax bill.
